# Summary & Logic
This document specifies the multiple imputation models used to handle missing 
data in our daily diary study of pain interference predictions. We employed two-level 
predictive mean matching (2l.pmm) via the mice package in R, which preserves the 
multilevel structure of repeated daily assessments nested within participants [Wijesuriya et al 2025](https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.10274). 

Our imputation strategy was informed by Missing At Random (MAR) diagnostics presented 
in the companion supplementary material (MAR_explore_documentation), which identified 
systematic patterns in missingness that we address through careful predictor selection. 

We present two imputation specifications:

1. Primary model (imp_1): Standard specification based on theoretical relationships and general imputation practice
2. Sensitivity model (imp_2): Adds lagged predictors to address specific MAR patterns identified in diagnostics

This leads to two predictor matrices differing **only** by the inclusion of `lagged_interf_worry`
as a predictor of morning worry. We call the reference predictor matrix "pred" and the alternative
predictor matrix with addition of `lagged_interf_worry` named "pred_b".

# Load pre-processed day-level EMA data

# Imputation
```{r eval=T, echo=FALSE}

data_set_b4mice <- data_set_b4mice %>% 
  group_by(alias) %>%  
  arrange(day_count) %>%
  mutate(
    lagged_interf_worry = lag(interf_worry, 1),
    lagged_daily_average_pain = lag(daily_avg_pain, 1)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Identify complete and incomplete variables
complete.vars<-names(data_set_b4mice)[colSums(is.na(data_set_b4mice)) == 0]
incomplete.vars<-names(data_set_b4mice)[colSums(is.na(data_set_b4mice)) != 0]

# in mice the id variable is required to be integer format
data_set_b4mice$alias <- as.integer(data_set_b4mice$alias)  # Convert alias to integer

# Define imputation methods
meth1 <- make.method(data_set_b4mice)
meth1[complete.vars] <- ""  # No imputation for complete variables
meth1[incomplete.vars] <- "2l.pmm" # Two-level predictive mean matching for incomplete variables
meth1[c("lagged_interf_worry", "lagged_daily_average_pain")] <- ""  # No imputation for the lag variables


# Define predictor Matrix
pred <- make.predictorMatrix(data_set_b4mice)

# Set all to 0 first
pred[,] <- 0

# with "0" we tell which variables are not predictors
# leaving blank the row means all rows
#pred["predicted","predictor"]
pred[,c("alias","Sex","Education")] <- 0

# time-fixed variable should not be imputed using time
# all time fixed variables are complete in this case
pred[c("Age"), c("day_count")] <- 0

# Specify alias as cluster variable
pred[, "alias"] <- -2  # Cluster grouping variable


# To specify random slopes for a predictor in a univariate imputation model for a certain variable, 
# number “2” should be included in the corresponding column variable for the row variable that 
# is being imputed. 
# In the case the time variable explains less than 0.1% of variance in most variables. 
# Adding day_count as Random slopes in this imputation model should account for meaningful 
# heterogeneity in the effect of a Day_count across individuals but this is not the case here:
#   Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod']
#   Formula: evening_interference ~ interf_worry + day_count + (1 + day_count |      alias)
#      Data: model_data
#   
#   REML criterion at convergence: 1374.7
#   
#   Scaled residuals: 
#       Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
#   -3.2540 -0.6005  0.0373  0.6560  3.5467 
#   
#   Random effects:
#    Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev. Corr
#    alias    (Intercept) 0.537136 0.73290      
#             day_count   0.001493 0.03864  0.81
#    Residual             3.186085 1.78496   

# Var explained by daycount across individuals is 0.04%: 
# 0.001493/(3.186085 + 0.001493 + 0.537136) = 0.0004008361 

# Therefore allowing alias-specific variability in the slope does not appreciably 
# improve the fit or capture meaningful heterogeneity for my imputation model.
# Conclusion: remove day_count as random slope to improve model fit stability and to
# allow for a simpler model
#pred[incomplete.vars),"day_count"] <- 2 

# ===== INTERF_WORRY (morning) =====
pred["interf_worry", c("day_count", 
                       "morning_pain", "morning_mood", "morning_stress", 
                       "daily_avg_interference", "Age")] <- 1
                      
# ===== MORNING_PAIN =====
pred["morning_pain", c("day_count", "morning_mood", "morning_stress", 
                       "daily_pain_variability", "Age")] <- 1

# ===== MORNING_MOOD =====
pred["morning_mood", c("day_count", "morning_pain", "morning_stress",
                       "daily_mood_variability", "Age")] <- 1

# ===== MORNING_STRESS =====
pred["morning_stress", c("day_count", "morning_pain", "morning_mood",
                         "daily_stress_variability", "Age")] <- 1

# ===== EVENING_INTERFERENCE (outcome) =====
pred["evening_interference", c("day_count", "interf_worry", 
                                "daily_avg_pain", "daily_avg_stress", 
                                "daily_avg_mood", "Age")] <- 1

# ===== DAILY_AVG_INTERFERENCE (auxiliary) =====
pred["daily_avg_interference", c("day_count", "daily_avg_pain",
"daily_avg_stress", "daily_avg_mood")] <- 1



```

The reference MICE model runs with "pred" and attain model `imp_1`.

## imputation 1

```{r eval=FALSE}
set.seed(200720)
imp_1 = mice(data = data_set_b4mice, 
            m = 28, 
            predictorMatrix = pred, 
            method = meth1, 
            maxit = 12)

#saveRDS(imp_1, "c:/Documents and Settings/d.vitali/Desktop/Github/CRIISP-WP6/Data/imputation_m28_12_05_25.rds")
```

The alternative reference MICE model runs with "pred_b" and attain model `imp_1`.
All other variables use identical predictor specifications as the primary model.

By including lagged worry as a predictor of current worry, we condition the 
imputation model on a variable that explains missingness patterns, potentially 
reducing bias under MAR assumptions. The comparison between models assesses how 
robust are our downstream findings (Q2) to this specification choice.

## imputation 2

```{r eval=FALSE}

pred_b<-pred

pred_b["interf_worry", c("day_count", 
                       "lagged_interf_worry",
                       "morning_pain", "morning_mood", "morning_stress", 
                       "daily_avg_interference", "Age")] <- 1


diff_matrix <- (pred_b != pred) 

diff_pos <- which(diff_matrix, arr.ind = TRUE)


# Show how many differences
n_diff <- nrow(diff_pos)

# Show positions (with dimnames)
rownames_diff <- rownames(pred)[diff_pos[,"row"]]
colnames_diff <- colnames(pred)[diff_pos[,"col"]]

data.frame(
  row = rownames_diff,
  col = colnames_diff,
  pred_a = pred[diff_pos],
  pred_b = pred_b[diff_pos]
)


imp_2 = mice(data = data_set_b4mice, 
            m = 28, 
            predictorMatrix = pred_b, 
            method = meth1, 
            maxit = 12)

#saveRDS(imp_2, "c:/Documents and Settings/d.vitali/Desktop/Github/CRIISP-WP6/Data/imputation_m28_2026_02_09.rds")
```



## IMP_1 Convergence plots
We assessed convergence via trace plots of means/standard deviations across 28 
chains and iterations, plus density plots of imputed vs. observed values 
[van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn 2011](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v045.i03). Acceptable convergence requires:

* random chain mixing: We assess multiple MCMC chains to make sure that they explore the parameter space freely, that they interweave without separation or sticking, and we check whether the sampler gets "trapped" in local modes
* parameter stabilization: We expectet that means and standard deviations of imputed values plateau after initial burn-in iterations. This progressive "convergence" shows that the chains have forgotten initial values and reach sowewhat stationary posterior distributions.
* plausible imputed distributions: Densityplots should confirm that imputed values (red) have similar shape, spread, and range to observed data (blue). This means that the original features of the data like (e.g) the skewness in pain interference is preserved in the imputation datasets.


To extend this diagnostic we load the imputation with extendeded 20 iteration 
```{r echo=FALSE}
# Check convergence patterns
imp_1_ext<-readRDS("c:/Documents and Settings/d.vitali/Desktop/Github/CRIISP-WP6/Data/imputation_m28_20it_12_05_25.rds") 
imp_1<-readRDS("c:/Documents and Settings/d.vitali/Desktop/Github/CRIISP-WP6/Data/imputation_m28_12_05_25.rds") 

plot(imp_1_ext, c("interf_worry", "evening_interference", "morning_pain", 
              "morning_mood", "morning_stress"))
```

Trace plots show random intermingling with no trends/divergence, and stabilization by iterations 4-6

In addition we examine ([van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn 2011](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v045.i03)):

* densityplots: it is useful to show differences in kernel density estimates of the imputed and observed data
* bwplot: is useful to study the distributions in datasets. Gives a side-by-side box-and-whisker plots for the observed and synthetic data

```{r}
densityplot(imp_1_ext, ~ interf_worry + evening_interference + morning_pain + morning_mood + morning_stress)
```

Density plots showed imputed values (red) overlapping observed data and preserving skewness in pain interference

```{r}
bwplot(imp_1, interf_worry + evening_interference + morning_pain + morning_mood + morning_stress ~ .imp, pch = 20, cex = 1.2)
```

bwplot across all 28 imputations confirmed that imputed values fell within plausible ranges 
for both interf_worry and evening_interference (0-10 scale). Imputed values 
showed appropriate dispersion across the scale without clustering at extremes 
or producing impossible values. The evident overlap of red and blue boxplots
indicates that imputed values matched the distributional characteristics of 
observed data.


### Additional MAR Explore 

From ([van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn 2011](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v045.i03))

Bondarenko and Raghunathan [2016](https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/references.html#ref-BONDARENKO2016) proposed a more refined diagnostic tool that aims to compare the distributions of observed and imputed data conditional on the missingness probability. The idea is that under MAR the conditional distributions should be similar if the assumed model for creating multiple imputations has a good fit. 

If MAR assumption holds:

* Imputed values (filled circles) distributed similarly to observed values (open circles) across all propensity score levels
* No systematic separation between observed and imputed

If MAR does not hold:
* Imputed values cluster at different BMI levels than observed values with similar missingness probability
* Gap between filled and open circles suggests unobserved confounding
```{r}

# Predict probability that record has missing outcome (evening_interference)
# using observed morning predictors
fit <- with(imp_1, 
            glm(ici(imp_1) ~ interf_worry + morning_pain + 
                             morning_mood + morning_stress + day_count,
                family = binomial))

# Calculate propensity scores
ps <- rep(rowMeans(sapply(fit$analyses, fitted.values)), imp_1$m + 1)

# Plot evening_interference vs propensity score
xyplot(imp_1, evening_interference ~ ps | as.factor(.imp),
       xlab = "P(incomplete | observed morning variables)",
       ylab = "Evening Interference",
       pch = c(1, 19),  # 1=observed, 19=imputed
       col = mdc(1:2))

```

## IMP_2 convergence
Imp_2 differs from imp_1 by exactly ONE predictor (lagged_interf_worry for interf_worry). 
This is a narrow sensitivity check for later models, it is not a fundamentally different model 
and it does not require the same convergence testing.
